parts.name: Recovering depth
parts.blurb: What a camera keeps and what it destroys, and the first way to get the lost number back.

parts.name: Placing the cameras
parts.blurb: Rigid motion on a curved space, then pose by agreement: from scans, and from images alone.

parts.name: From points to pictures
parts.blurb: A surface you can query, a forward model that predicts pixels, and the exam that grades both.

parts.name: Fitting a scene by gradient
parts.blurb: Make visibility soft so photographs can supervise geometry; store the scene as a field; make it fast.

parts.name: Learning across scenes
parts.blurb: When views run out, priors; the networks that carry them; sampling instead of averaging.

parts.name: The world moves
parts.blurb: Add time, and hand the problem to world models.

lessons.title: A pixel is a ray
lessons.move: Read the camera as a function from rays to colors: a pixel fixes a direction and no distance, and parallax turns the missing distance into the shift between two views.
lessons.sum: Projection is many-to-one, so one image cannot say how far; but moving the camera shifts each pixel by f·b/Z, so the exam "predict the view from a new camera" is exactly the depth problem.

lessons.title: A second ray pins the point
lessons.move: Intersect two rays: disparity measures depth, the error grows as Z², the search is one-dimensional, and active sensors measure range directly.
lessons.sum: Triangulation and stereo, the Z² error law and the baseline trade-off, epipolar search, ToF and LiDAR error models, back-projection from a depth map to a point cloud.

lessons.title: Where is the camera? Rigid motion on a curved space
lessons.move: A pose is a rotation and a translation; rotations are a curved space, so take steps in the tangent space and map them back with the exponential.
lessons.sum: SO(3) and SE(3), why rotation matrices cannot be averaged and Euler angles lock, Rodrigues, exp and log, quaternions, and gradient steps that never leave the space.

lessons.title: Pose by agreement I: aligning scans
lessons.move: The right pose makes two scans coincide: closed form when matches are known (Procrustes), a match-then-solve loop when they are not (ICP).
lessons.sum: Kabsch/Procrustes with the reflection fix, ICP and its basin of attraction, point-to-plane, degeneracy, robust loss, and the first appearance of the explain-compare-update loop.

lessons.title: Pose by agreement II: images alone
lessons.move: With no depth sensor the rays themselves must meet: the epipolar constraint gives relative pose up to scale, and bundle adjustment polishes poses and points together.
lessons.sum: The essential matrix and the 8-point algorithm, the scale ambiguity, cheirality, RANSAC, bundle adjustment as the loop with a pinhole renderer, gauge freedom, and how SLAM is the same loop online.

lessons.title: From points to a surface
lessons.move: Fuse noisy depth maps by averaging in a signed distance field, then read the surface off its zero set (and a mesh off marching cubes).
lessons.sum: Why points fail the exam, what a surface must provide, TSDF fusion and its 1/sqrt(n) noise law, normals and sphere tracing, marching cubes, explicit versus implicit trade-offs.

lessons.title: What a pixel measures: the forward model and the exam
lessons.move: Write the forward model (first hit, then Lambert shading), score it on held-out cameras, and find the wall: visibility is a cliff in the geometry.
lessons.sum: Radiance along a ray, Lambertian color and why photometric matching works, visibility by rasterizing or ray casting, PSNR as the exam, and the boundary term that autodiff misses.

lessons.title: Making visibility soft: volume rendering
lessons.move: Replace the first hit with a fog of absorbing, emitting particles: transmittance, alpha compositing, and a hard surface as the sharp limit.
lessons.sum: Derive T(t) = exp(-∫σ) and C = ∫Tσc, discretize to alpha compositing, take the hard limit, differentiate it, and see long-range gradients.

lessons.title: Radiance fields: a scene as a function
lessons.move: Let a function of position (and direction) hold density and color, and train it by comparing rendered rays with photographs.
lessons.sum: The field, view dependence, positional encoding and spectral bias, sampling, bundle adjustment with a dense renderer, and why few views still ghost.

lessons.title: Speed: grids, hashes and Gaussian splats
lessons.move: Spend parameters only where the scene is: feature grids and hashes, then soft explicit primitives rendered by splatting.
lessons.sum: Where NeRF's time goes, feature grids and hash tables, 3D Gaussians and their projection, sorted alpha compositing, density control, and what splats cost.

lessons.title: When the views run out: learning across scenes
lessons.move: Add information from outside the data: a prior learned over many scenes, used inside geometry, instead of it, or amortized into one forward pass.
lessons.sum: Null spaces and ill-posedness, MAP and posterior uncertainty, hand-made versus learned priors, monocular depth and its scale ambiguity, learned matching, feed-forward reconstruction.

lessons.title: Networks that eat 3D
lessons.move: Respect the symmetry of the data: sets need order-free pooling, volumes need sparsity, driving scenes collapse to a bird's-eye view.
lessons.sum: Permutation invariance and PointNet, locality, sparse convolution and its cost, bird's-eye view, detection heads, and what a regression network cannot answer.

lessons.title: Sampling the unseen: generative 3D
lessons.move: Sample from the posterior instead of averaging it: distill a 2D prior, generate consistent views, or generate native 3D.
lessons.sum: Why the mean is not a valid object, mixture posteriors, score distillation and its failure modes, multiview generation, 3D latent diffusion, feed-forward generation.

lessons.title: When the scene moves: time, SLAM, and the road to world models
lessons.move: Add time: a canonical scene plus motion, a camera that moves too, and the hand-off from explaining the past to predicting the future.
lessons.sum: Dynamic scenes and their ambiguity, deformation fields, per-primitive trajectories, SLAM as the same loop online, and why reconstruction has no actions and no future.

batons.S00-01: The Computer Vision track taught the camera as a function: a 3D point goes in, a pixel comes out. Vision has to run it backwards — the pixels are what we have and the scene is what we want. What does one pixel tell us about the point that made it, and what does it leave out?
batons.S01-02: A pixel pins down a direction and nothing else: every point along its ray lands on the same pixel, so depth is the one number per pixel that the image destroys. It is also exactly the number a new viewpoint needs, because moving the camera sideways by b shifts a pixel by f·b/Z. So the shift between two views measures depth. How precisely can two rays pin down a point, and what limits that precision?
batons.S02-03: Two rays pin a point only because we were told where the second camera is. In practice that is the unknown: a robot, a phone or a scanner moves between measurements, and every depth map lives in its own sensor frame. To compare or merge frames we must write down a rotation and a translation, and a rotation cannot be added, averaged or stepped along like a vector. How do we describe a rigid motion so that a computer can estimate it?
batons.S03-04: A pose is now a rotation and a translation, and a small correction is a rotation vector applied through the exponential map, a step that never leaves the space of rotations. That says how to move, but not in which direction. Two scans of the same room, taken from unknown poses, must coincide where they overlap. How do we turn "the scans should coincide" into an equation we can solve for the pose?
batons.S04-05: Aligning scans has a closed-form answer when the matches are known, and a two-step loop when they are not: match each point to its nearest neighbour, solve, repeat. The loop converges to the nearest consistent answer if it starts close enough. All of it needs a sensor that measures 3D directly. A phone measures only pixels, so there is no scan to align. How can poses be recovered from images alone, and what plays the role of "the scans should coincide"?
batons.S05-06: Images alone give camera poses and a sparse set of 3D points, up to one global scale, by adjusting both until the points reproject onto the pixels. That is the first model we fitted by comparing its prediction with the data. Now test it on the job it is for: predict a photograph from a camera we did not use. Points show through one another and nothing exists between them. What must a model of geometry provide to answer "what does this ray hit?", and how is it built from noisy depth?
batons.S06-07: Fusing noisy depth into a signed distance field gives a surface that answers "where is the first hit along this ray?", with a normal and an inside and an outside. But the held-out photograph is made of colors, not positions, and so far nothing has a color. What does a pixel actually measure, and how do we write down, and score, the image a model predicts?
batons.S07-08: We can render a model and score it against a photograph, but we cannot yet improve it by gradient: where one surface hides another, a pixel is a cliff in the geometry, so the loss is flat almost everywhere and says nothing about which way to move. What would a renderer look like whose pixels change smoothly with the scene, and still reduce to the hard one when the scene is solid?
batons.S08-09: Volume rendering makes every pixel a smooth function of the density and color along its ray, and a solid surface is simply its sharp limit. It still leaves the unknown: a density and a color at every point of space, which gradient descent on photographs must find, in a function class flexible enough for fine detail and smooth enough to train. What should that function be?
batons.S09-10: A radiance field trained on photographs can reproduce views it never saw, but only after a long training run, and each pixel costs hundreds of evaluations of a large network, almost all of them in empty space. Where is the waste, and what representation spends its effort only where the scene is?
batons.S10-11: Grids and Gaussians fit one scene in minutes and draw it in real time, but only by being shown that scene from many views. Give them three views, or one, and the unseen part is unconstrained: they score well on the photographs they were fitted to and fail the exam. Where can the missing information come from, if not from more photographs?
batons.S11-12: The missing information comes from a prior learned over many scenes, and a prior has to live in a network. But a 3D input is not an image: a point cloud is an unordered set, a voxel grid is almost entirely empty, a LiDAR sweep has a different length every time. What must a network respect to learn from 3D data, and what can it then answer?
batons.S12-13: A trained network returns one answer per input, the average of everything compatible with what it saw. That is fine for "where is the car" and wrong for "what is behind the mug": the average of two plausible backs is a back that cannot exist. How do we produce a scene that agrees with the data and is also a valid sample of the kinds of scenes there are?
batons.S13-14: We can now reconstruct a scene, learn what scenes look like, and invent the parts nobody saw. But the scene holds still. In the world things move and so do we, and a model that explains the past cannot say what happens next or what would happen if we pushed. What does it take to represent a scene that changes, and then to predict it?
batons.S14-x: A scene that changes can be reconstructed from what has already happened. An agent that has to act needs the other direction: what will happen next, and what would happen if it did something else. Nothing in a reconstruction answers that, because it has no actions and no future. What must a model carry in its head to answer "if I do this, what happens next?", and why would an agent want one at all?
